title: India’s microfinance recovery hinges on the debt borrowers can actually repay
summary: RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu described a modest recovery in Indian microfinance and challenged lenders to show that larger loans were affordable. Speaking on 13 November in remarks published on 15 November, he acknowledged an industry request to raise the household income threshold for eligibility. The RBI would assess whether a review was needed. He took a firmer position on proposals to loosen the debt-service calculation. Allowing lenders to omit principal repayments on certain loans would hide cash obligations that still fall due. The speech announced no increase in either limit (paragraphs 6–11).

The 2022 framework applies across regulated lenders. A household earning up to ₹300,000 annually is eligible, with monthly repayments capped at 50% of household income. Murmu argued that the ceiling leaves little scope for error when earnings are vulnerable to economic or weather shocks and savings are low. A study he cited put average repayments at 18.7% of monthly income and consumption at nearly two-thirds. A separate NABARD rural survey put consumption and other expenses at about three-quarters. The rural survey is a proxy for microfinance customers. Neither average describes the household at the cap or establishes that it could take on more debt (paragraph 11 and footnotes 6–7).

The question matters at scale. Credit bureau figures cited in the speech put the active borrower base at 66 million in June 2026. Average loans had been getting larger while smaller loans lost ground. For a lender, larger repeat loans could signal that experienced borrowers had accumulated usable credit histories. Murmu also identified less favourable explanations. Part of a new loan could be refinancing an old one, or the income recorded at application could have been overstated. A portfolio can increase in value while extending formal credit to fewer first-time customers. The address provided no estimate of the share attributable to each explanation (paragraphs 2 and 20).

Pricing and collections create a second test of the recovery. Murmu said lending rates were rising across categories of regulated entities, partly because of credit costs in preceding quarters. Lenders retain discretion under board-approved models that account for funding and risk and include internal ceilings on rates and charges. He saw scope for more competitive pricing and warned that undisclosed charges, bundled products or harsh recovery practices could undermine customer retention. A signed disclosure provided weak evidence of understanding if field staff had failed to explain the terms in the borrower’s language. Because the model relies on field staff, unresolved employee grievances could also disrupt credit delivery (paragraphs 12–21).

The reliability of the underlying credit record affects all these judgements. Lenders must now submit credit information at least four times each month, up from fortnightly reporting. Some banks had placed microfinance loans in the consumer segment. Bureaus were advised to move those records and close that reporting option. Reclassification can change what an underwriter sees about an applicant’s total obligations without any new borrowing. The rural credit scores developed by credit information companies were still being evaluated by lenders. Murmu also supported collective safeguards developed by self-regulatory bodies, while reserving interpretation of RBI rules to the regulator (paragraphs 22–27). For an investor assessing asset quality, the direction of loan growth alone cannot resolve the issues he raised about refinancing, underwriting or the cost of collecting repayments.

questions.question: How much growth in average loan size represented refinancing of existing debt?
questions.detail: Murmu describes stronger lending to established borrowers and identifies the possibility of debt repayment using new loans. Compare repeat-loan vintages, previous balances, disbursement proceeds and days between settlement and renewal. The credit bureau reports cited in footnotes 2 and 8, together with lender disclosures, provide a starting point. Replacing an old loan can keep payments current for a time while giving little evidence of improving household cash flow.

questions.question: What share of borrowers had little income left after essentials and scheduled repayments?
questions.detail: The cited studies describe averages, while the regulatory limit applies household by household. Examine the distribution of repayments and essential spending by region, season and loan size, including principal on debts from other lenders. The NCAER borrowing study and NABARD household surveys cited in the speech could inform that work. A portfolio concentrated near the limit could be sensitive to even a temporary income shock despite a benign sector average.

questions.question: Are reported asset quality and loan pricing comparable across lenders?
questions.detail: The speech reports both higher lending rates and inconsistent bureau classification. Reconcile reporting changes and customer migrations before comparing vintages across banks and non-bank lenders. Then compare effective rates, fees, provisions, collections and complaints in statutory disclosures. This could distinguish a lender with improving risk-adjusted revenue from one passing past losses to borrowers whose future repayment capacity remains uncertain.
